content: Indication-Specific Dosing for Panax Ginseng Oral Dosing: 6–3 grams orally, once daily to three times daily. 3 grams orally, once daily to three times daily. 900 mg orally, three times daily. 200 mg orally, once daily. 100–300 mg of standardized extract (7% ginsenosides), three times daily for 3–4 weeks. Topical Use: Cream applied topically 1 hour prior to intercourse and washed off before intercourse. Therapeutic Effects and Uses Adaptogen: Panax ginseng is used to help the body adapt to internal and external stressors, combat fatigue, and enhance stamina. Potential Benefits: Anxiety reduction. Enhancement of athletic and physical stamina. Improvement in cognitive function. Alleviation of depression. Male fertility support. Relief from headaches. Immunostimulant properties. Reduction of menopausal hot flashes. Treatment of impotence. Possibly Effective For: Cognitive function improvement. Diabetes management. Erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation. Possibly Ineffective For: Athletic performance enhancement. Menopausal symptoms. General quality of life improvement. Insufficient Evidence For: Breast cancer. Bronchitis. Cancer. Common cold. Congestive heart failure. Influenza. Drug Interactions Anticoagulation Effects: Panax ginseng has been shown to increase anticoagulation effects when combined with various drugs and substances. Caution and close monitoring are advised when used with the following: Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): Aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, celecoxib, naproxen, ketoprofen, indomethacin, meloxicam, and others. Anticoagulants and Antiplatelet Agents: Warfarin, heparin, enoxaparin, dabigatran, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, and others. Herbal Supplements: Garlic, ginger, ginkgo biloba, cinnamon, dong quai, devil’s claw, and others. Pharmacodynamic Synergism: Panax ginseng may enhance the effects of certain medications through pharmacodynamic synergism. These include: Antidepressants: Amitriptyline, fluoxetine, sertraline, duloxetine, venlafaxine, and others. Insulin and Antidiabetic Agents: Insulin aspart, insulin glargine, insulin lispro, and others. Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs): Phenelzine, isocarboxazid, tranylcypromine, and others. Unclear Interactions: Panax ginseng may interact with substances like mistletoe and nettle, which have opposing effects on anticoagulation. The clinical significance of these interactions is not well understood, and caution is advised. Pregnancy and Lactation The safety of Panax ginseng during pregnancy and lactation has not been well established. Use should be avoided unless specifically recommended by a healthcare provider. Adverse Effects Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, headache, and insomnia. Rare but serious effects may include allergic reactions or interactions leading to excessive anticoagulation. Clinical Recommendations Monitoring: Patients taking Panax ginseng in combination with anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, or other interacting drugs should be closely monitored for signs of bleeding or other adverse effects. Caution: Use caution when combining Panax ginseng with medications that have similar pharmacodynamic effects, as this may potentiate their actions. Individualized Therapy: Dosage and use should be tailored to the individual patient’s needs, taking into account their medical history and concurrent medications.
